title: Spatio-Temporal Graph Learning via State-Space Models
one_liner: Encode both graph structure and time into a memory system so distant nodes and long-ago events shape today's predictions.
lead: Graphs change over time: friendship networks grow and shrink, financial transactions come and go, sensor readings shift. To predict what happens next, a model must track both nearby changes and distant patterns across long time spans. Most models only remember the immediate neighbors and recent events, missing the big picture.

problem.h2: Graphs change, but models only see one step
paras: Real-world graphs are not static pictures. A social network grows with new friendships; an interaction network has messages that arrive at different times; sensor readings drift. To predict a future link (will Alice friend Bob?), a model must understand the full history and distant structure.

A beginner tries a simple approach: for each prediction, scan only the immediate neighbors (Alice's current friends) and the recent history (what happened in the last few steps). This works for nearby patterns but collapses on long-range questions. For example, if Bob keeps appearing in conversations five steps ago, but that signal is buried in intermediate noise, the model forgets. Or if the prediction depends on a friend-of-a-friend pattern three hops away, scanning only one-hop neighbors misses it.

callout.html: Models fail to remember distant events and to track structures beyond immediate neighbors.

paras: The paper changes the memory update rule. Instead of a simple local aggregation ("average your neighbors' signals"), it uses a polynomial projection through the graph Laplacian, so the update simultaneously encodes: which time step we are at, and how many hops each piece of information has traveled.

hidden.name: multi-hop structural distance
paras: The Laplacian polynomial naturally encodes the shortest path between any two nodes. A polynomial of degree k captures paths up to k hops. When you multiply the Laplacian by itself, you get information about two-hop neighbors; multiply again and you get three hops, and so on. The paper uses this to build a memory that knows both temporal distance (how long ago) and structural distance (how far in the graph) for every piece of information.

The paper estimates this quantity by examining the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix and deriving how the polynomial projection distorts the state over time. This is mathematically exact, not learned.

heat.caption: Hotter cells have information that is both recent and close (low distance). Dim cells hold old or distant signals.

reads.html: The Laplacian polynomial keeps a record of which information (which node, which time) is near or far from the query.
The continuous-time topology-aware HiPPO reformulation projects the solution through a polynomial of the Laplacian matrix, maintaining a basis that orthogonalizes both temporal and spatial structure.

mechanism.h2: Why encoding structure and time together works
paras: Without merging structure and time, the model has two separate channels: a temporal memory (what happened when) and a graph aggregation (who-is-connected-to-whom). When trying to predict a link, it may ask "what signal came from Alice five steps ago?" and separately ask "how many hops is Alice from Bob?" but never ask "has the signal from Alice had time to propagate five hops to reach Bob?" This mismatch means long-range dependencies stay invisible.

The Laplacian polynomial fixes this by treating them as one system. A coefficient in the polynomial says: "this information travels k hops at speed s." So if Bob is three hops from Alice and the information took five steps to travel, the polynomial coefficient at that degree automatically dampens or amplifies that path based on whether it is realistic. This means the model learns to trust long-range patterns when they are actually possible and to ignore noise when they are not. The memory state update becomes a single coherent operation: project the entire state through the polynomial, and every entry automatically gets the right weight for its spatio-temporal distance.

stages.s: Coefficients encode distance: both time and hops
Distant signals are weighted by probability

math.words: The new state is the old state multiplied by a polynomial of the graph Laplacian matrix, scaled by time.
symbols: the state vector (memory) at time t
a polynomial of degree k, where L is the Laplacian matrix, scaled by time t
the graph Laplacian matrix (encodes which nodes connect)
the current time step (how long this edge has existed)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have a tiny graph with 3 nodes. L = [[2, -1, -1], [-1, 2, -1], [-1, -1, 2]] (each node connects to two others).
We use a degree-2 polynomial: P_k(x) = 1 + x + 0.5*x^2.
At time t=1: P_k(1*L) = I + L + 0.5*L^2. This matrix mixes: one-hop paths (L term) and two-hop paths (L^2 term).
If state s(0) = [1, 0, 0] (all signal at node 1), then s(1) = P_k(L) * [1, 0, 0] spreads the signal to nodes 2 and 3, weighted by their distance.
By t=5, the polynomial at higher degree captures paths that take many hops, so node 1's signal has a small but non-zero contribution to nodes far away.

math.note: The polynomial naturally balances how much a distant piece of information contributes: distant information comes from higher-degree terms, which have smaller weight.

charts.title: Short-range problems (neighbors only)
charts.note: Both methods work when the answer is nearby. This paper is slightly better because it still encodes structure cleanly.

charts.title: Long-range problems (multi-hop + history)
charts.note: When predictions depend on distant nodes or old events, the Laplacian polynomial remembers what old approaches forget.

items.b: Graph structure changes, but polynomial is fixed.
items.html: If the graph topology itself rewires (new edges appear, old ones vanish), the Laplacian changes. The polynomial was designed for a static graph structure. The paper does not address online graph rewiring; it assumes the topology is mostly stable.

To capture long-range paths, the polynomial degree must grow. Computing the polynomial with a large degree requires matrix multiplications that scale with the matrix size. On huge graphs with millions of nodes, this becomes slow.

items.b: Selecting the right polynomial degree requires tuning.
items.html: If k is too small, long-range patterns are missed. If k is too large, the model overfits and becomes slow. Practitioners must guess the right k per dataset, and the paper does not provide a principled way to choose it.

items.b: Done right: static, medium-sized graphs with long-range dependencies.
items.html: Use this method when the graph structure is stable, the number of nodes is manageable (hundreds to tens of thousands), and you need to predict links or classify nodes based on distant history and multi-hop patterns.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny dynamic graph with 10 nodes, add edges randomly over 50 time steps. Create synthetic ground truth: two specific nodes at time t=30 are connected if there was a path through 4 hops at time t=10. A one-hop model (baseline) cannot see 4 hops and predicts random; this paper's model should detect the pattern and predict correctly.
demo.closing: The demo should show: on short-range dependencies (up to 2 hops), both methods tie; on long-range (at 4 hops), this paper's accuracy is visibly higher (e.g. 75% vs 50%), proving the Laplacian polynomial actually captures distance.
